evidence_quotes.quote: O objetivo deste artigo é analisar alguns aspectos da relação entre população e recursos hídricos. Investiga a percepção cultural e usos locais da água para compreender de que formas tais costumes dialogam ou conflitam com as normas legais e técnicas propostas pelas agências reguladoras do recurso.
Em sua grande maioria, aquelas são formadas por consumidores diretos, enquanto a população urbana consome água por meio da empresa que a trata e distribui.

Embora no seu período de vigência a lei pouco tenha influenciado consumo e costumes —raras bacias têm comitê instituído ou negociado— a redefinição das normas legais sobre recursos hídricos estimulou a organização de interesses que envolvem empresas e Estado.
Ao todo, no período 1999/2002 foram pesquisadas 22 comunidades e entrevistadas 188 famílias rurais.

Como o objetivo do estudo não era quantificar escassez ou abundância do recurso, não houve preocupação com análise estatística. Buscava-se compreender percepções e atitudes, informações fundamentalmente qualitativas.

criterion_notes.c1: Fails C1 (and matches Exclusion Criterion 7: water-resource studies unrelated to household or community service access). The study investigates rural peasant populations' cultural perceptions and direct use of natural water resources (springs, creeks, and rivers) for mixed agrarian (garden irrigation, livestock, stills) and domestic self-supply. The authors explicitly distinguish these rural 'direct consumers' of natural water sources from urban populations served by water treatment and distribution utilities (p. 141). Mentions of municipal water trucks, cisterns, and relocation to rural villages appear only peripherally as last-resort coping responses when springs dry up, without examining water or sanitation service access.
criterion_notes.c2: Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, C2 is 'no': the paper does not examine any rule-type legal, regulatory, or administrative mechanism directly governing water or sanitation service access (such as eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation or tenure requirements for service, utility tariffs/cost recovery, regulatory enforcement, or utility ownership/structure). Instead, it contrasts informal peasant cultural norms around natural springs ('água-dom', customary sharing of springs) with macro bulk water-resource management under Brazil's 1997 Water Law (Lei nº 9.433/1997, river basin committees, ANA, and bulk water abstraction permits/charges for hydroelectric and irrigation users). Under the plain broad wording of Criterion 2, the paper discusses water-resource governance and customary institutional norms in general terms (so plain C2 read in isolation on resource governance could be viewed as 'yes'), but the authors explicitly state that Lei nº 9.433/1997 and river basin committees had scarcely been instituted or influenced local consumption during the study period (p. 134, p. 142), and the study still fails C1 because it concerns natural water-resource management rather than water or sanitation service access; therefore plain_criterion2_decision is also 'exclude'.
criterion_notes.c3: Satisfies C3. Contains qualitative primary empirical evidence from fieldwork conducted in 1999–2002 across 22 rural communities and 188 rural families in six municipalities of the Jequitinhonha Valley, Minas Gerais, using paired semi-structured family interviews and community meetings (pp. 130–131). Qualitative socio-legal/ethnographic methods are fully eligible in principle.
criterion_notes.c4: Fails C4 for service access. As the authors note (p. 131), the empirical study aimed to understand qualitative cultural perceptions, classifications ('água fina' vs. 'água grande'), and customary practices regarding natural water resources rather than water or sanitation service-access outcomes. Although it qualitatively describes household coping with ecological drying of springs (3-day rotation at springs, women's collection distances, abandoning home gardens, occasional fallback to municipal water trucks or cisterns, and moving to villages), it reports no water or sanitation service-access outcomes linked to a service rule or institution.
criterion_notes.c5: Satisfies C5 as a reporting gate: the population and unit of analysis (188 rural families across 22 communities in 6 municipalities), qualitative study design (semi-structured interviews plus community discussions), and ethnographic focus/findings are clearly identifiable from the full text.
criterion_notes.c6: Satisfies C6: full text is in Portuguese, which is directly eligible without translation under Criterion 9.

study_design: Qualitative field study (semi-structured family interviews and community meetings)
population_and_sample: 188 rural farming families across 22 rural communities in 6 municipalities (Turmalina, Veredinha, Medina, Joaíma, Monte Formoso, and Jequitinhonha) in the Jequitinhonha Valley, Minas Gerais (1999–2002)
exposure: Customary peasant norms and cultural perceptions of natural springs and streams contrasted with Brazil's 1997 National Water Resources Policy (Lei nº 9.433/1997, river basin committees, ANA, and bulk water permits/charges)
outcome: Cultural perceptions and classifications of natural water quality and scarcity, customary spring-sharing practices, and household agrarian/domestic adaptations to drying springs (abandoning irrigated gardens, women's water-fetching burden, fallback water trucks/cisterns, and migration to villages)
rationale: Exclude (E01: Wrong topic). Full-text Portuguese article matches the metadata (Ribeiro & Galizoni, 2003). Based on qualitative fieldwork with 188 rural families across 22 communities in the Jequitinhonha Valley, Minas Gerais (1999–2002), the paper investigates peasant cultural perceptions and customary management of natural water resources (springs, creeks, and rivers used directly for gardens, livestock, and household needs) and contrasts this 'water-as-gift' worldview with macro water-resource governance under Brazil's 1997 Water Law (Lei nº 9.433/1997, river basin committees, ANA, and bulk water abstraction permits for hydroelectric and irrigation users). It is a natural water-resources and watershed-governance study rather than a study of household or community water or sanitation service access (Exclusion Criterion 7 / fails C1), and it does not empirically examine any rule-type legal, regulatory, or administrative mechanism governing service access (fails C2; moreover, the authors note that Lei nº 9.433/1997 and basin committees had scarcely been instituted or affected local practices during the study period). Under both the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading and the plain wording of Criterion 2, the study is excluded.
